title: The SOLID principles
idea: SOLID is five rules for classes: one reason to change, extend without editing, honour the parent's contract, keep interfaces small, depend on abstractions.

analogy.text: A wall socket: the kettle needs only the socket's shape, any plug that fits works, and a new appliance never needs rewiring the house.
analogy.breaks: Sockets never change; real interfaces do, so design them with care.

points: Single responsibility (SRP): a class has one reason to change.
Open/closed (OCP): add behaviour with a new class, not by editing old ones.
Liskov substitution (LSP): a subtype must keep every promise its parent type makes.
Interface segregation (ISP) keeps interfaces small; dependency inversion (DIP) makes callers depend on them.

steps.caption: SRP: `Checkout` only runs a payment. Printing the result is the job of a separate `Receipt`.
DIP: `Checkout` depends only on the `Receipt` interface. `main` injects a `ConsoleReceipt` through the constructor.
`pay(1200, card)` asks the `PaymentMethod` to charge. `Checkout` never checks which class it got.
OCP: `WalletPayment` came later as a new class. Not one line of `Checkout` changed.
LSP: the wallet declines 900 by returning `false`, as the contract allows. It never throws a surprise.
ISP: `Receipt` has one method. A class that only prints never has to fake payment methods.

code.title: S, O, I and D
code.caption: A checkout built on two small interfaces. New payment methods arrive as new classes.

walk.text: DIP: the abstraction `Checkout` depends on. `false` is a normal answer, not an error.
OCP: each method is its own class. Adding one never edits `Checkout`.
ISP: `Receipt` asks for one method, so any printer fits easily.
SRP: one job. DIP: it holds a `Receipt`, injected through the constructor.
`pay` calls the interface only. It works for any `PaymentMethod`.

code.title: L, broken
code.caption: `FrozenSettings` compiles as a `Settings`, yet it breaks code that trusts `put`.

walk.text: The interface promises both reading and writing.
This subtype refuses `put`: it type-checks but breaks the promise.
`rename` was written for any `Settings` and now fails on one.
Same call, two subtypes, one broken promise. The fix is ISP: split read from write.

pitfalls: Do not throw `UnsupportedOperationException` from an override; split the interface instead.
Do not split classes by method count; split them by who asks for changes.
Add an interface where you need to swap or fake a class, not by reflex.

quiz.q: What is the second line `LspDemo` prints?
quiz.why: `FrozenSettings.put` throws `UnsupportedOperationException` with the message `frozen`. `rename` catches it and returns that message, so substitution failed.
quiz.code:
rename(new FrozenSettings());
// rename: s.put("name", "shop") ... catch -> "broke: " + message

takeaway: Small classes, small interfaces, kept promises: add features by adding classes.
